1.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I sat in mine house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, that the hand of the Lord God fell there upon me. Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber. And he put forth the form of an hand, and took me by a lock of mine head; and the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the inner gate that looketh toward the north; where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provoketh to jealousy. And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, according to the vision that I saw in the plain. Then said he unto me, Son of man, lift up thine eyes now the way toward the north. So I lifted up mine eyes the way toward the north, and behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry. He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch measure the interval at a year and two months from the call, set out the sequence of idolatry seen, city smitten and sanctuary forsaken, and reason from the prophet's station that the image stood outside the entrance; Ellicott infers from the opening line that a priest already known as a prophet was held in regard among the exiles and had a house of his own, explains the elders' title by who the captives mostly were, denies that the fiery figure is the earlier vision returning since that bursts on the prophet later inside the temple, notes how carefully likeness, appearance and form are repeated to keep the whole visionary, holds that the prophet never left Chaldea, identifies the gate as the northern one leading up from the people's court to the priests', distinguishes the glory here from the old glory that filled the house, and reads the threat as a bare infinitive with no subject that might mean the removal of the people but is truer to the vision as the removal of God from his own sanctuary.

Gill puts the date in the sixth year of the captivity in the month answering to late summer, corrects the versions that read a fifth month, thinks the day a sabbath, reports versions reading a likeness of a man where the text has fire and finds the human form implied by loins and a hand, takes the hand that lifts the prophet for the Spirit sent by Christ, and says the presence had not withdrawn though provoked, so that an idol set where God himself was measures the insolence; Calvin insists the man did not move and only seemed to himself seized by the Spirit, says the same of the hand, which is a likeness and not a hand, warns against imagining a real journey between earth and sky, rejects the rendering that makes the last word of the description angel since it means colour, and treats the reappearance of the glory as a seal on the message that arms a man with hard heads to deal with.

Clarke admires the device by which idolatry is personified and made an idol, named from the provocation it gives, and lists the candidates for the image, a Baal set up by an apostate king, the god of war, or the youth beloved by the goddess of love, giving the case for the last since that youth was killed by a boar sent in jealousy by the goddess's other lover; Wesley supposes the elders came to keep the day or to ask what would become of their brethren, identifies the fiery figure with the man seen on the throne and hears wrath in the fire, marks the passage down to the sixteenth verse as vision only, takes the image for an idol set up, destroyed and set up again by successive reigns, explains its name from the affront to a God who had married the nation to himself, and adds of the departing glory that nobody intended it though nothing else could be expected.
Henry makes the same calculation of the date and explains why a man in Babylon is shown Jerusalem, since captives reckoned their peace and trouble by the city's.

debates.question: What is the fiery figure the prophet sees?

positions.position: Not the earlier vision returning, since that bursts on the prophet later inside the temple; the repeated likeness, appearance and form keep it visionary.
The same man seen on the throne, with wrath heard in the fire.
A human form, implied by loins and hand, which some versions read as a likeness of a man where the text has fire.

debates.question: What was the image of jealousy?

positions.position: Probably the youth beloved by the goddess of love, since he was killed by a boar sent in jealousy by her other lover, which fits the name exactly; a Baal of an apostate king or the god of war are the alternatives.
An idol set up, destroyed and set up again by successive reigns, named from the affront to a God who had married the nation to himself.
Its position can be fixed from the prophet's station: it stood outside the entrance.

outliers.claim: Presses that no bodily journey took place at all: the man did not move, only seemed to himself seized, and the hand that lifted him was a likeness and not a hand.
Explains why a man already in Babylon is shown Jerusalem, since captives reckoned their own peace and trouble by the city's.

themes: And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I sat in mine house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, that the hand of the Lord God fell there upon me.

Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber.

And he put forth the form of an hand, and took me by a lock of mine head; and the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the inner gate that looketh toward the north; where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provoketh to jealousy.
And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, according to the vision that I saw in the plain.

Then said he unto me, Son of man, lift up thine eyes now the way toward the north. So I lifted up mine eyes the way toward the north, and behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry.

He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations.

7.pericope_label: And he brought me to the door of the court; and when I looked, behold a hole in the wall. Then said he unto me, Son of man, dig now in the wall: and when I had digged in the wall, behold a door. And he said unto me, Go in, and behold the wicked abominations that they do here. So I went in and saw; and behold every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, pourtrayed upon the wall round about. And there stood before them seventy men of the ancients of the house of Israel, and in the midst of them stood Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, with every man his censer in his hand; and a thick cloud of incense went up. Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth.

schools.summary: Ellicott cannot fix the place, which is clearly not where the prophet had been standing and must lie somewhere between that and the north gate of the outer enclosure, though the older building record names no courts beyond the inner and the outer; he agrees the painted rites are Egyptian and argues the case carefully, since creature worship existed elsewhere and painting idols on walls is elsewhere credited to a Chaldean import while the combination here is thoroughly Egyptian and the politics of the moment point the same way; he doubts any chamber about the courts could have held seventy men and reminds the reader that a scene given in vision for instruction need not be possible in every detail, denies that these were the council since it did not exist until after the return, refers the number instead to the seventy who once went up with Moses, and distinguishes this secret creature worship from the ordinary open idolatry of the nation.

Gill reports the identification of the place with the eastern gate, the commonest entrance and the one where the council sat, so that what the prophet sees is their own chamber painted round with figures, takes the creeping things for beetles and the like worshipped as gods, and treats the doubled question as a demand that the prophet weigh what he has seen; Calvin makes the whole action visionary and reads its meaning off the geography, since an idol in one part of the temple would have been intolerable but a defilement running through every part shows a people past recovery, agrees that the standing seventy of the old constitution are not meant and takes the word for elders as an office rather than an age while allowing that the number alludes to that order, explains that the question is put to the prophet so that he may pass sentence as a judge and leave the guilty without plea, and notes that the men are not named out of any respect but reproved the harder, since a corruption that starts with elders drags everyone after it.

Clarke notes that the hole was too small to see through and had to be enlarged before anything could be observed, lists the likely painted subjects, the ox and ape and dog, the crocodile, the ibis and the beetle, compares the walls of tombs in that country where such figures still appear, and identifies the father of the one man named as an officer of the temple whose place the son probably inherited, putting him at the head of the band; Wesley identifies what the opening leads to as a private door by which the priests went in to their images, takes the creeping things for whatever the neighbouring nations adored, calls the worshippers heads of tribes and families who should have been examples and were ringleaders, observes that the father of the man named had been forward in a reformation while the son is as forward in corruption, and states the excuse the worshippers gave themselves, that a God who does not see them is a God they may replace.

Henry notices the method of the disclosure, that the prophet is not set down at once in the chamber of images but led toward it by stages, partly so that he should have to search the thing out for himself and partly so that he should feel how carefully such discoveries have to be made.

debates.question: Who were the seventy men in the chamber?

positions.position: Not the council, which did not exist until after the return; the number looks back to the seventy who went up with Moses.
Not the standing seventy of the old constitution either; elders here is an office rather than an age, though the number alludes to that order.
Heads of tribes and families, who should have been examples and were ringleaders instead.

debates.question: Where in the temple precinct was the door the prophet was shown?

positions.position: Unfixable: not where he had been standing, and somewhere short of the north gate of the outer enclosure, though the building record names no courts between.
The eastern gate, the commonest entrance and the seat of the council, so that the painted chamber was their own.
A private door by which the priests went in to their images.

outliers.claim: Reads the meaning off the geography: an idol in one part of the temple would have been intolerable, but a defilement running through every part shows a people past recovery.
Makes the digging part of the point, since the hole was too small to see through and had to be enlarged before anything could be observed.

themes: And he brought me to the door of the court; and when I looked, behold a hole in the wall.
Then said he unto me, Son of man, dig now in the wall: and when I had digged in the wall, behold a door.
And he said unto me, Go in, and behold the wicked abominations that they do here.
So I went in and saw; and behold every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, pourtrayed upon the wall round about.

And there stood before them seventy men of the ancients of the house of Israel, and in the midst of them stood Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, with every man his censer in his hand; and a thick cloud of incense went up.

Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth.

13.pericope_label: He said also unto me, Turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations that they do. Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the Lord’s house which was toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz. Then said he unto me, Hast thou seen this, O son of man? turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations than these. And he brought me into the inner court of the Lord’s house, and, behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the porch and the altar, were about five and twenty men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord, and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east. Then he said unto me, Hast thou seen this, O son of man? Is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they commit the abominations which they commit here? for they have filled the land with violence, and have returned to provoke me to anger: and, lo, they put the branch to their nose. Therefore will I also deal in fury: mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: and though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch draw the contrast that organises the vision, that the men represented by the seventy worshipped in secret chambers while the women sat at the temple gate and mourned in public, and report that Jerome, with Melito and the Greek fathers, read the mourned name as Adonis, treating that identification as correct; Ellicott explains why the Greek name could not stand in the Hebrew text, since in that form it means Lord and is used of God, gives the five and twenty as the heads of the twenty-four courses with the high priest standing for the priesthood as the elders stood for the people, presses the wording as it were rather than about as a phrase belonging to vision, fixes the spot between porch and altar as the court's most sacred ground, calls the gesture with the branch an allusion to a lost custom and offers the Parsee habit of holding twigs before the mouth as the simplest guess, and reads the refusal to hear as the day of grace outrun, the chapter's chief lesson.

Gill identifies the northern gate as the one little used of several and observes that idolatry told worse where the Lord was most solemnly served, and says none but priests might come into the inner court; Calvin doubts the mourning rite reached Judaea since the lamentation is attested in Greece and Asia Minor rather than the neighbouring regions and prefers the Egyptian figure wept for yearly by neighbours from whom the Jews had taken other rites, treats the scene as a sin peculiar to women and finds in it the depth reached by women taught the law from childhood, takes the number of sun-worshippers as a round one for an uncertain, refuses to make their sin one of error since the law forbidding that worship gave its reason that the lights were made for our service, weighs the turned back heaviest as contempt rather than mere denial, takes the word for violence as a part standing for every breach of the second table and finds the intolerable thing in the order, that having despised men they attacked God, and guards the closing threat by distinguishing prayer that springs from faith, which is never rejected, from the tumult necessity wrings from unbelief, with the elect excepted.

Clarke follows the identification of the mourned figure with the youth of the Greek story, adds the report that the Lebanon stream ran red at the festival and explains it as ochre in swollen water rather than sympathy, gives the five and twenty as the twenty-four courses with the high priest and reads their eastward posture as Persian sun worship, and takes the branch at the nose for boughs carried in procession while refusing the filthier constructions; Wesley offers two readings of the comparative, that the later sins are greater because added to the rest or because some circumstance makes them so, settling on place as the holier ground, sets the mourning at the outer court so called because women were admitted, reads the turned back as contempt of God and his worship, and compares the branch to the wreathed staff of the wine-god's worshippers.

Henry notes that the prophet had seen enough already and is twice told to turn again, draws from it that those who live retired do not know what wickedness the world holds, and reports that the mourners shed idolatrous tears at the very door in defiance of the sacred rites, with debasing practices going along with the mourning.

debates.question: Who is the figure the women mourned?

positions.position: The youth of the Greek story, as Jerome and the Greek fathers read it; the Greek name itself could not stand in Hebrew because that form means Lord and is used of God.
More probably the Egyptian figure, since the lamentation is attested in Greece and Asia Minor rather than in the neighbouring regions, and other Egyptian rites had already been taken up.

debates.question: What is meant by putting the branch to the nose?

positions.position: Boughs carried in procession, as branches figured widely in Gentile ceremony; the filthier constructions are not worth repeating.
An allusion to a custom now lost, best guessed from the Parsee habit of holding twigs before the mouth.
The wreathed staff waved by the worshippers of the wine-god.

outliers.claim: Guards the closing refusal to hear by distinguishing prayer that springs from faith, which is never rejected, from the tumult necessity wrings from unbelief, and excepts the elect from the general body.
Observes that the sin told worse for its setting, since the northern gate was where the sacrifices were offered and the inner court was ground no one but priests might enter.
